diagram_name: From the Schism to the Sack, 1054–1261
chapter_title: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
learning_objective: The learner will explain how earlier events from 1054 to 1203 led to the sack of Constantinople in 1204, by choosing the earlier event that best explains each of four later events, with at least 3 of 4 correct.
specification:
Type: timeline **sim-id:** schism-to-sack-timeline
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** explain
**Learning Objective:** The learner will explain how earlier events from 1054 to 1203 led to the sack of Constantinople in 1204, by choosing the earlier event that best explains each of four later events, with at least 3 of 4 correct. **Prerequisites:** Crusades, Great Schism of 1054, Fourth Crusade, Republic of Venice, Byzantine Empire, Seljuk Turks (defined in Parts Six and Seven above, and in Chapter 3). **Evidence of Mastery:** After exploring the timeline, the learner answers four cause questions in the Feedback section. An answer is correct when it matches the correct option listed. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. **Misconceptions:** (1) The Fourth Crusade set out to attack Constantinople. (2) The Great Schism of 1054 was a single clean break that all Christians felt at once. (3) The Crusades were a single war. (4) Venice and Byzantium were always enemies. **Instructional Rationale:** Explaining causes requires seeing events in order and in relation. A clickable timeline lets the learner read each event's description in sequence, and the cause questions require the learner to connect a later event to its most direct earlier cause rather than recall dates. **Content:** Each event has a date, a title, a description shown when the event is clicked, and a group. Groups: "Church" (Ch), "Crusades" (Cr), "Byzantium and Venice" (BV). | # | Date | Group | Title | Description shown on click | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 1054-07-16 | Ch | Excommunication in Hagia Sophia | Cardinal Humbert lays a bull of excommunication on the altar; Patriarch Keroularios replies in kind. A symbol of the long drift between Rome and Constantinople. | | 2 | 1071-08-26 | BV | Battle of Manzikert | The Seljuk Turks defeat the Byzantine army in eastern Anatolia; much of Anatolia is lost over the next decades. | | 3 | 1082 | BV | Venice's trading privileges | Alexios I grants Venice tax-free trade and a quarter on the Golden Horn in return for naval help (some historians date the grant to 1092). | | 4 | 1095-11-27 | Cr | Urban II at Clermont | Answering Alexios I's request for soldiers, the pope calls for an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem. | | 5 | 1096 to 1097 | Cr | Crusaders at Constantinople | Crusader armies camp outside the city; Alexios ferries them across the Bosphorus. | | 6 | 1099-07-15 | Cr | Jerusalem taken | The First Crusade captures Jerusalem; crusader states are founded. | | 7 | 1147 to 1149 | Cr | Second Crusade | Fails at Damascus. | | 8 | 1171-03-12 | BV | Venetians arrested | Emperor Manuel I arrests Venetians across the empire and seizes their goods; relations break down. | | 9 | 1182 | BV | Massacre of the Latins | A mob in Constantinople kills or drives out most of the city's Western merchants. | | 10 | 1187-10-02 | Cr | Saladin takes Jerusalem | After his victory at Hattin, Saladin takes Jerusalem. | | 11 | 1189 to 1192 | Cr | Third Crusade | Acre retaken; Jerusalem remains under Saladin. | | 12 | 1202-11 | Cr | Zara taken | Unable to pay Venice for its fleet, the crusaders capture the Christian city of Zara for Venice; the pope excommunicates them. | | 13 | 1203-07 | Cr | First attack on Constantinople | The crusaders restore Isaac II and his son Alexios IV, who has promised them 200,000 marks he cannot pay. | | 14 | 1204-04-12 to 1204-04-15 | Cr | Sack of Constantinople | The crusaders storm the city and sack it for three days; churches, palaces and Hagia Sophia are looted. | | 15 | 1204-05-16 | BV | Latin emperor crowned | Baldwin of Flanders is crowned emperor in Hagia Sophia; Venice takes three-eighths of the city and empire. | | 16 | 1205 | BV | Dandolo buried in Hagia Sophia | The Doge of Venice dies and is buried in the church's gallery. | | 17 | 1261-07-25 | BV | Constantinople recovered | Forces of Michael VIII Palaiologos retake the city; the Latin Empire ends. | **Provenance:** Dates and descriptions from Part Six and Part Seven of this chapter, cross-checked against the Wikipedia articles "Crusades", "Fourth Crusade", "East–West Schism" and "Massacre of the Latins". The 1082 date is given with its alternative because historians disagree. **Rules:** The timeline spans 1050 to 1265. All 17 events are present from the start. Clicking an event shows its title, date and description. Point events (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17) are shown as points; events with a date range (5, 7, 11, 14) are shown as ranges. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the three groups and sees the full span from 1054 to 1261. 2. The learner clicks events in date order and reads each description. 3. The learner answers the four cause questions. 4. The learner should notice that the Church, Crusades, and Byzantium-and-Venice groups converge in 1202 to 1204. **Feedback:** Four multiple-choice questions, shown in this order, each answered once for scoring: 1. "Why did crusader armies first come to Constantinople in 1096?" Options: (a) Alexios I had asked the pope for soldiers after losing Anatolia to the Seljuks [correct]; (b) They planned to capture the city; (c) Venice hired them. Correct message: "Yes: the Crusades began as an answer to Byzantium's request for help." Incorrect message: "Look at events 2 and 4: Manzikert, then Alexios's request." 2. "Why did the crusaders attack Zara, a Christian city, in 1202?" Options: (a) To pay their debt to Venice for the fleet [correct]; (b) Because of the Schism of 1054; (c) The pope ordered it. Correct: "Right: the debt to Venice redirected the crusade." Incorrect: "Look at event 12: the pope in fact excommunicated them for it." 3. "Why were many Byzantines hostile to Westerners in the city by 1203?" Options: (a) The arrests of 1171 and the massacre of 1182 had poisoned relations [correct]; (b) The First Crusade had taken Jerusalem; (c) Saladin had taken Jerusalem. Correct: "Yes: a generation of conflict over trade came before the crusade." Incorrect: "Look at events 8 and 9." 4. "Why did the crusaders storm the city in April 1204?" Options: (a) Alexios IV could not pay the 200,000 marks he had promised them [correct]; (b) The pope ordered the attack; (c) Constantinople had attacked Venice. Correct: "Right: a broken promise of money, on top of Venice's debts, led to the assault." Incorrect: "Look at event 13." Score >= 3 shows "You can explain how a crusade to Egypt ended in Constantinople." Score < 3 shows "Click events 8 to 14 again, in order, and try the questions once more." Answers are revealed after each question. **Starting State:** The whole span 1050 to 1265 is visible with all 17 events, and a prompt: "The Fourth Crusade set out for Egypt. How did it end in Constantinople?" **Chapter Anchors:** 1054 excommunication on July 16; Manzikert 1071; Clermont November 1095; Jerusalem 1099; Saladin 1187; Zara 1202; sack April 12 to 15, 1204; Venice's three-eighths share; Dandolo buried 1205; recovery 1261; Alexios IV's promise of 200,000 marks; four questions; mastery 3 of 4.
